entities.name: Anagni Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Cathedral of Santa Maria Annunziata in Anagni, Italy, built 1073-1104 CE in the Romanesque style, is famous primarily as the site of the 'Slap of Anagni' (Schiaffo di Anagni) — the September 7, 1303 confrontation where agents of King Philip IV of France (including Guillaume de Nogaret) seized Pope Boniface VIII in his chamber in Anagni (Boniface's hometown), physically manhandled him, and held him prisoner for three days before townspeople freed him. Boniface died a month later; the incident was the turning point that ended papal political supremacy over European monarchs.

Boniface VIII had issued the papal bull Unam Sanctam (1302) — the most extreme claim of papal supremacy over secular rulers, asserting that 'every human creature' was subject to the Roman pontiff 'as necessary for salvation.' Philip IV of France (who had been taxing French clergy without papal consent) refused this claim; Nogaret's 1303 assault on Boniface was Philip's answer. Whether Boniface was actually slapped (the 'Slap' may be legendary) is disputed, but his physical humiliation by French agents — and his death a month after release — ended the era of medieval papal political supremacy.

The cathedral's interior contains extraordinary 12th-13th century fresco cycles in the crypt — considered among the finest Romanesque fresco programs in Italy — painted by the 'Cosmati' school (named for the mosaic-paving Roman families). The Cathedral Treasury includes remarkable medieval goldsmith works. The cathedral's Romanesque facade with sculpted portal is one of the most complete examples of Lazio Romanesque.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Anagni Cathedral — where agents of the French king physically seized the pope who had declared himself sovereign over all rulers — is the site where medieval papal political supremacy died in 1303, making a small Lazio town's cathedral one of the most historically consequential buildings in the history of church-state relations.
